A measurement tool scored the draft on how it carries feeling. For each measure below it gives the current value and a target. Revise the essay so that its measures move to the targets; the tool will score the result again.
- positive charge (hedons per 1,000 words): now 112.5, target 114.6. Counts positive words such as good, love, fun.
- negative charge (dolors per 1,000 words): now 22.8, target 5.9. Counts negative words such as bad, hate, problem.
- words that carry charge (% of words): now 33.3, target 32.4. Counts share of all words that carry any feeling.
- charge under a negation (% of charge): now 3.5, target 3.8. Counts feeling words placed under not, never or n't.
- charge after an intensifier such as 'very' (% of charge): now 0.0, target 3.2. Counts feeling words placed right after very, really or so.
- charge after a contrast word such as 'but' (% of charge): now 0.0, target 0.0. Counts feeling words placed after but or however in the same sentence.
- net charge of the last fifth minus the text's mean (per 1,000 words): now 60.0, target -16.6. Counts how much more positive the last fifth is than the essay as a whole; negative means a more downbeat ending.
- how unevenly charge is spread over sentences (1 = as if words were dealt at random): now 1.4, target 1.3. Counts above 1 means the feeling is bunched into some sentences while others are plain; below 1 means it is spread evenly.

Draft:

Dear Principal,

I believe Policy 1 is the better choice. Letting students have phones during lunch and free time, as long as they are off in class, gives us the benefits of phones without the biggest problems.

First, phones are a safety tool. If there is an emergency, a late bus, or a change in after-school plans, students can reach their families right away. A total ban would remove that option, and many parents would worry about it.

Second, Policy 1 teaches responsibility. Students will have to decide for themselves when a phone is appropriate. Learning to put a phone away when it is time to focus is a skill we will need in college and at work. If phones are banned completely, we never get the chance to practice it.

Third, a full ban would be very hard to enforce. Teachers would spend time searching for hidden phones and arguing with students, and that takes time away from teaching. Under Policy 1, the rule is simple and fair: phones are off during class. Students who break it can lose their phone privileges.

Lunch is also the one time we can relax, check on family, or talk with friends. That break helps us concentrate better in the afternoon.

For these reasons, I hope you will choose Policy 1.

Sincerely,
A Concerned Student
